entries.76a3b324a7eb7f8b213677767342ebbc8c3c5b19: <div sID="gen9882" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Job.27" sID="Job.27"/> <div eID="gen9882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9883" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9884" type="x-p"/> Job had sometimes complained of his friends that they were so eager in disputing that they would scarcely let him put in a word: "Suffer me that I may speak;" and, "O that you would hold your peace!" But now, it seems, they were out of breath, and left him room to say what he would. Either they were themselves convinced that Job was in the right or they despaired of convincing him that he was in the wrong; and therefore they threw away their weapons and gave up the cause. Job was too hard for them, and forced them to quit the field; for great is the truth and will prevail. What Job had said (<reference osisRef="Job.26.1-Job.26.14">ch. xxvi.</reference>) was a sufficient answer to Bildad's discourse; and now Job paused awhile, to see whether Zophar would take his turn again; but, he declining it, Job himself went on, and, without any interruption or vexation given him, said all he desired to say in this matter. I. He begins with a solemn protestation of his integrity and of his resolution to hold it fast, <reference osisRef="Job.27.2-Job.27.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. II. He expresses the dread he had of that hypocrisy which they charged him with, <reference osisRef="Job.27.7-Job.27.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. He shows the miserable end of wicked people, notwithstanding their long prosperity, and the curse that attends them and is entailed upon their families, <reference osisRef="Job.27.11-Job.27.23">ver. 11-23</reference>.
entries.4645f7013c186389746e836885ae4fba111a6ea5: <div eID="gen9884" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9883" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Protestation of His Sincerity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9885" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 <hi type="italic">As</hi> God liveth, <hi type="italic">who</hi> hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, <hi type="italic">who</hi> hath vexed my soul; <hi type="super">3</hi> All the while my breath <hi type="italic">is</hi> in me, and the spirit of God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in my nostrils; <hi type="super">4</hi> My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit. <hi type="super">5</hi> God forbid that I should justify you: till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. <hi type="super">6</hi> My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach <hi type="italic">me</hi> so long as I live. <div eID="gen9885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9886" type="x-p"/> Job's discourse here is called a <hi type="italic">parable (mashal</hi>), the title of Solomon's proverbs, because it was grave and weighty, and very instructive, and he spoke as one having authority. It comes from a word that signifies <hi type="italic">to rule,</hi> or <hi type="italic">have dominion;</hi> and some think it intimates that Job now triumphed over his opponents, and spoke as one that had baffled them. We say of an excellent preacher that he knows how <hi type="italic">dominari in concionibus—to command his hearers.</hi> Job did so here. A long strife there had been between Job and his friends; they seemed disposed to have the matter compromised; and therefore, since an <hi type="italic">oath for confirmation is an end of strife</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.16">Heb. vi. 16</reference>), Job here backs all he had said in maintenance of his own integrity with a solemn oath, to silence contradiction, and take the blame entirely upon himself if he prevaricated. Observe, <div eID="gen9886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9887" type="x-p"/> I. The form of his oath (<reference osisRef="Job.27.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment.</hi> Here, 1. He speaks highly of God, in calling him <hi type="italic">the living God</hi> (which means <hi type="italic">everliving,</hi> the eternal God, that has life in himself) and in appealing to him as the sole and sovereign Judge. We can swear by no greater, and it is an affront to him to swear by any other. 2. Yet he speaks hardly of him, and unbecomingly, in saying that he had taken away his judgment (that is, refused to do him justice in this controversy and to appear in defence of him), and that by continuing his troubles, on which his friends grounded their censures of him, he had taken from him the opportunity he hoped ere now to have of clearing himself. Elihu reproved him for this word (<reference osisRef="Job.34.5">ch. xxxiv. 5</reference>); for God is righteous in all his ways, and takes away no man's judgment. But see how apt we are to despair of favour if it be not shown us immediately, so poor-spirited are we and so soon weary of waiting God's time. He also charges it upon God that he had <hi type="italic">vexed his soul,</hi> had not only not appeared for him, but had appeared against him, and, by laying such grievous afflictions upon him had quite embittered his life to him and all the comforts of it. We, by our impatience, vex our own souls and then complain of God that he has vexed them. Yet see Job's confidence in the goodness both of his cause and of his God, that though God seemed to be angry with him, and to act against him for the present, yet he could cheerfully commit his cause to him. <div eID="gen9887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9888" type="x-p"/> II. The matter of his oath, <reference osisRef="Job.27.3-Job.27.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. 1. That he would not <hi type="italic">speak wickedness, nor utter deceit</hi>—that, in general, he would never allow himself in the way of lying, that, as in this debate he had all along spoken as he thought, so he would never wrong his conscience by speaking otherwise; he would never maintain any doctrine, nor assert any matter of fact, but what he believed to be true; nor would he deny the truth, how much soever it might make against him: and, whereas his friends charged him with being a hypocrite, he was ready to answer, upon oath, to all their interrogatories, if called to do so. On the one hand he would not, for all the world, deny the charge if he knew himself guilty, but would declare the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and take to himself the shame of his hypocrisy. On the other hand, since he was conscious to himself of his integrity, and that he was not such a man as his friends represented him, he would never betray his integrity, nor charge himself with that which he was innocent of. He would not be brought, no, not by the rack of their unjust censures, falsely to accuse himself. If we must not bear false witness against our neighbour, then not against ourselves. 2. That he would adhere to this resolution as long as he lived (<reference osisRef="Job.27.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the while my breath is in me.</hi> Our resolutions against sin should be thus constant, resolutions for life. In things doubtful and indifferent, it is not safe to be thus peremptory. We know not what reason we may see to change our mind: God may reveal to us that which we now are not aware of. But in so plain a thing as this we cannot be too positive that we will never speak wickedness. Something of a reason for his resolution is here implied—that our breath will not be always in us. We must shortly breathe our last, and therefore, while our breath is in us, we must never breathe wickedness and deceit, nor allow ourselves to say or do any thing which will make against us when our breath shall depart. The breath in us is called <hi type="italic">the spirit of God,</hi> because he breathed it into us; and this is another reason why we must not speak wickedness. It is God that gives us life and breath, and therefore, while we have breath, we must praise him. <div eID="gen9888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9889" type="x-p"/> III. The explication of his oath (<reference osisRef="Job.27.5-Job.27.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">God forbid that I should justify you</hi> in your uncharitable censures of me, by owning myself a hypocrite: no, <hi type="italic">until I die I will not remove my integrity from me; my righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go.</hi>" 1. He would always be an honest man, would hold fast his integrity, and not curse God, as Satan, by his wife, urged him to do, <reference osisRef="Job.2.9">ch. ii. 9</reference>. Job here thinks of dying, and of getting ready for death, and therefore resolves never to part with his religion, though he had lost all he had in the world. Note, The best preparative for death is perseverance to death in our integrity. "<hi type="italic">Until I die,</hi>" that is, "though I die by this affliction, I will not thereby be put out of conceit with my God and my religion. <hi type="italic">Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.</hi>" 2. He would always stand to it that he was an honest man; he would not remove, he would not part with, the conscience, and comfort, and credit of his integrity; he was resolved to defend it to the last. "God knows, and my own heart knows, that I always meant well, and did not allow myself in the omission of any known duty or the commission of any known sin. This is my rejoicing, and no man shall rob me of it; I will never lie against my right." It has often been the lot of upright men to be censured and condemned as hypocrites; but it well becomes them to bear up boldly against such censures, and not to be discouraged by them nor think the worse of themselves for them; as the apostle (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">Heb. xiii. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have a good conscience in all things, willing to live honestly.</hi> <div eID="gen9889" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9890"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9891"/>Hic murus aheneus esto, nil conscire sibi.<l eID="gen9891" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9892"/>Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence,<l eID="gen9892" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9893"/>Still to preserve thy conscious innocence.<l eID="gen9893" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9890"/> <div sID="gen9894" type="x-p"/> Job complained much of the reproaches of his friends; but (says he) <hi type="italic">my heart shall not reproach me,</hi> that is, "I will never give my heart cause to reproach me, but will keep a conscience void of offence; and, while I do so, I will not give my heart leave to reproach me." <hi type="italic">Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifies.</hi> To resolve that our hearts shall not reproach us when we give them cause to do so is to affront God, whose deputy conscience is, and to wrong ourselves; for it is a good thing, when a man has sinned, to have a heart within him to smite him for it, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.10">2 Sam. xxiv. 10</reference>. But to resolve that our hearts shall not reproach us while we still hold fast our integrity is to baffle the designs of the evil spirit (who tempts good Christians to question their adoption, <hi type="italic">If thou be the Son of God</hi>) and to concur with the operations of the good Spirit, who witnesses to their adoption.
entries.98d3d1af8828bb23383fe17d59afb6ec5ab62535: <div eID="gen9894" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Condition of Hypocrites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9895" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous. <hi type="super">8</hi> For what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained, when God taketh away his soul? <hi type="super">9</hi> Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? <hi type="super">10</hi> Will he delight himself in the Almighty? will he always call upon God? <div eID="gen9895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9896" type="x-p"/> Job having solemnly protested the satisfaction he had in his integrity, for the further clearing of himself, here expresses the dread he had of being found a hypocrite. <div eID="gen9896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9897" type="x-p"/> I. He tells us how he startled at the thought of it, for he looked upon the condition of a hypocrite and a wicked man to be certainly the most miserable condition that any man could be in (<reference osisRef="Job.27.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let my enemy be as the wicked,</hi> a proverbial expression, like that (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.19">Dan. iv. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">The dream be to those that hate thee.</hi> Job was so far from indulging himself in any wicked way, and flattering himself in it, that, if he might have leave to wish the greatest evil he could think of to the worst enemy he had in the world, he would wish him the portion of a wicked man, knowing that worse he could not wish him. Not that we may lawfully wish any man to be wicked, or that any man who is not wicked should be treated as wicked; but we should all choose to be in the condition of a beggar, an out-law, a galley-slave, any thing, rather that in the condition of the wicked, though in ever so much pomp and outward prosperity. <div eID="gen9897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9898" type="x-p"/> II. He gives us the reasons of it. <div eID="gen9898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> 1. Because the hypocrite's hopes will not be crowned (<reference osisRef="Job.27.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">For what is the hope of the hypocrite?</hi> Bildad had condemned it (<reference osisRef="Job.8.13-Job.8.14">ch. viii. 13, 14</reference>), and Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.11.20">ch. xi. 20</reference>), and Job here concurs with them, and reads the death of the hypocrite's hope with as much assurance as they had done; and this fitly comes in as a reason why he would not remove his integrity, but still hold it fast. Note, The consideration of the miserable condition of wicked people, and especially hypocrites, should engage us to be upright (for we are undone, for ever undone, if we be not) and also to get the comfortable evidence of our uprightness; for how can we be easy if the great concern lie at uncertainties? Job's friends would persuade him that all his hope was but the hope of the hypocrite, <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">ch. iv. 6</reference>. "Nay," says he, "I would not, for all the world, be so foolish as to build upon such a rotten foundation; for <hi type="italic">what is the hope of the hypocrite?</hi>" See here, (1.) The hypocrite deceived. <hi type="italic">He has gained,</hi> and he has hope; this is his bright side. It is allowed that he has gained by his hypocrisy, has gained the praise and applause of men and the wealth of this world. Jehu gained a kingdom by his hypocrisy and the Pharisees many a widow's house. Upon this gain he builds his hope, such as it is. He hopes he is in good circumstances for another world, because he finds he is so for this, and he blesses himself in his own way. (2.) The hypocrite undeceived. He will at last see himself wretchedly cheated; for, [1.] God shall <hi type="italic">take away his soul,</hi> sorely against his will. <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy soul shall be required of thee.</hi> God, as the Judge, takes it away to be tried and determined to its everlasting state. He shall then fall into the hands of the living God, to be dealt with immediately. [2.] What will his hope be then? It will be vanity and a lie; it will stand him in no stead. The wealth of this world, which he hoped in, he must leave behind him, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Ps. xlix. 17</reference>. The happiness of the other world, which he hoped for, he will certainly miss of. He hoped to go to heaven, but he will be shamefully disappointed; he will plead his external profession, privileges, and performances, but all his pleas will be overruled as frivolous: <hi type="italic">Depart from me, I know you not.</hi> So that, upon the whole, it is certain that a formal hypocrite, with all his gains and all his hopes, will be miserable in a dying hour. <div eID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> 2. Because the hypocrite's prayer will not be heard (<reference osisRef="Job.27.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will God hear his cry when trouble comes upon him?</hi> No, he will not; it cannot be expected he should. If true repentance come upon him, God will hear his cry and accept him (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 18</reference>); but, if he continue impenitent and unchanged, let him not think to find favour with God. Observe, (1.) Trouble will come upon him, certainly it will. Troubles in the world often surprise those that are most secure of an uninterrupted prosperity. However, death will come, and trouble with it, when he must leave the world and all his delights in it. The judgment of the great day will come; fearfulness will surprise the hypocrites, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa. xxxiii. 14</reference>. (2.) Then he will cry to God, will pray, and pray earnestly. Those who in prosperity slighted God, either prayed not at all or were cold and careless in prayer, when trouble comes will make their application to him and cry as men in earnest. But, (3.) Will God hear him then? In the troubles of this life, God has told us that he will not hear the prayers of those who regard iniquity in their hearts (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.19">Ps. lxvi. 19</reference>) and set up their idols there (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">Ezek. xiv. 4</reference>), nor of those who turn away their ear from hearing the law, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Get you to the gods whom you have served,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 14</reference>. In the judgment to come, it is certain, God will not hear the cry of those who lived and died in their hypocrisy. Their doleful lamentations will all be unpitied. <hi type="italic">I will laugh at your calamity.</hi> Their importunate petitions will all be thrown out and their pleas rejected. Inflexible justice cannot be biassed, nor the irreversible sentence revoked. See <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22-Matt.7.23">Matt. vii. 22, 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.26">Luke xiii. 26</reference>, and the case of the foolish virgins, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.11">Matt. xxv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> 3. Because the hypocrite's religion is neither comfortable nor constant (<reference osisRef="Job.27.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Will he delight himself in the Almighty?</hi> No, not at any time (for his delight is in the profits of the world and the pleasures of the flesh, more than in God), especially not in the time of trouble. <hi type="italic">Will he always call upon God?</hi> No, in prosperity he will not call upon God, but slight him; in adversity he will not call upon God but curse him; he is weary of his religion when he gets nothing by it, or is in danger of losing. Note, (1.) Those are hypocrites who, though they profess religion, neither take pleasure in it nor persevere in it, who reckon their religion a task and a drudgery, a weariness, and snuff at it, who make use of it only to serve a turn, and lay it aside when the turn is served, who will call upon God while it is in fashion, or while the pang of devotion lasts, but leave it off when they fall into other company, or when the hot fit is over. (2.) The reason why hypocrites do not persevere in religion is because they have no pleasure in it. Those that do not delight in the Almighty will not always call upon him. The more comfort we find in our religion the more closely we shall cleave to it. Those who have no delight in God are easily inveigled by the pleasures of sense, and so drawn away from their religion; and they are easily run down by the crosses of this life, and so driven away from their religion, and will not always call upon God.
entries.06f231ea4744f1cfc2f3e7719471ae5ff568b132: <div eID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Heritage of the Wicked. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> I will teach you by the hand of God: <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> with the Almighty will I not conceal. 12 Behold, all ye yourselves have seen <hi type="italic">it;</hi> why then are ye thus altogether vain? <hi type="super">13</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, <hi type="italic">which</hi> they shall receive of the Almighty. <hi type="super">14</hi> If his children be multiplied, <hi type="italic">it is</hi> for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread. <hi type="super">15</hi> Those that remain of him shall be buried in death: and his widows shall not weep. <hi type="super">16</hi> Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay; <hi type="super">17</hi> He may prepare <hi type="italic">it,</hi> but the just shall put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on, and the innocent shall divide the silver. <hi type="super">18</hi> He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth <hi type="italic">that</hi> the keeper maketh. <hi type="super">19</hi> The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered: he openeth his eyes, and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not. <hi type="super">20</hi> Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night. <hi type="super">21</hi> The east wind carrieth him away, and he departeth: and as a storm hurleth him out of his place. <hi type="super">22</hi> For <hi type="italic">God</hi> shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand. <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">Men</hi> shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place. <div eID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> Job's friends had seen a great deal of the misery and destruction that attend wicked people, especially oppressors; and Job, while the heat of disputation lasted, had said as much, and with as much assurance, of their prosperity; but now that the heat of the battle was nearly over he was willing to own how far he agreed with them, and where the difference between his opinion and theirs lay. 1. He agreed with them that wicked people are miserable people, that God will surely reckon with cruel oppressors, and one time or other, one way or other, his justice will make reprisals upon them for all the affronts they have put upon God and all the wrongs they have done to their neighbours. This truth is abundantly confirmed by the entire concurrence even of these angry disputants in it. But, 2. In <hi type="italic">this</hi> they differed—they held that these deserved judgments are presently and visibly brought upon wicked oppressors, that <hi type="italic">they travail with pain all their days,</hi> that in prosperity <hi type="italic">the destroyer comes upon them,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">shall not be rich,</hi> nor their <hi type="italic">branch green,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">their destruction shall be accomplished before their time</hi> (so Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.15.20-Job.15.21">ch. xv. 20, 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.29">29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">32</reference>), that the <hi type="italic">steps of their strength shall be straitened,</hi> that <hi type="italic">terrors shall make them afraid on every side</hi> (so Bildad, <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">ch. xviii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">11</reference>), that he himself <hi type="italic">shall vomit up his riches,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits,</hi> so Zophar, <reference osisRef="Job.20.15">ch. xx. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">22</reference>. Now Job held that, in many cases, judgments do not fall upon them quickly, but are deferred for some time. That vengeance strikes slowly he had already shown (<reference osisRef="Job.21.1-Job.21.34">ch. xxi.</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.24.1-Job.24.25">xxiv.</reference>); now he comes to show that it strikes surely and severely, and that reprieves are no pardons. <div eID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> I. Job here undertakes to set this matter in a true light (<reference osisRef="Job.27.11-Job.27.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will teach you.</hi> We must not disdain to learn even from those who are sick and poor, yea, and peevish too, if they deliver what is true and good. Observe, 1. What he would teach them: "<hi type="italic">That which is with the Almighty,</hi>" that is, "the counsels and purposes of God concerning wicked people, which are hidden with him, and which you cannot hastily judge of; and the usual methods of his providence concerning them." This, says Job, <hi type="italic">will I not conceal.</hi> What God has not concealed from us we must not conceal from those we are concerned to teach. <hi type="italic">Things revealed belong to us and our children.</hi> 2. How he would teach them: <hi type="italic">By the hand of God,</hi> that is, by his strength and assistance. Those who undertake to teach others must look to the hand of God to direct them, to open their ear (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>), and to open their lips. Those whom God teaches with a strong hand are best able to teach others, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa. viii. 11</reference>. 3. What reason they had to learn those things which he was about to teach them (<reference osisRef="Job.27.12">v. 12</reference>), that it was confirmed by their own observation—<hi type="italic">You yourselves have seen it</hi> (but what we have heard, and seen and known, we have need to be taught, that we may be perfect in our lesson), and that it would set them to rights in their judgment concerning him—"<hi type="italic">Why then are you thus altogether vain,</hi> to condemn me for a wicked man because I am afflicted?" Truth, rightly understood and applied, would cure us of that vanity of mind which arises from our mistakes. That particularly which he offers now to lay before them is <hi type="italic">the portion of a wicked man with God,</hi> particularly of <hi type="italic">oppressors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.13">v. 13</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">ch. xx. 29</reference>. Their portion in the world may be wealth and preferment, but their portion with God is ruin and misery. They are above the control of any earthly power, it may be, but the Almighty can deal with them. <div eID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> II. He does it, by showing that wicked people may, in some instances, prosper, but that ruin follows them in those very instances; and that is their portion, that is their heritage, that is it which they must abide by. <div eID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> 1. They may prosper in their children, but ruin attends them. <hi type="italic">His children</hi> perhaps <hi type="italic">are multiplied</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.27.14">v. 14</reference>) or <hi type="italic">magnified</hi> (so some); they are very numerous and are raised to honour and great estates. Worldly people are said to be <hi type="italic">full of children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>), and, as it is in the margin there, <hi type="italic">their children are full.</hi> In them the parents hope to live and in their preferment to be honoured. But the more children they leave, and the greater prosperity they leave them in, the more and the fairer marks do they leave for the arrows of God's judgments to be levelled at, his three sore judgments, <hi type="italic">sword, famine, and pestilence,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13">2 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>. (1.) Some of them shall die by the sword, the sword of war perhaps (they brought them up to live by their sword, as Esau, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">Gen. xxvii. 40</reference>, and those that do so commonly die by the sword, first or last), or by the sword of justice for their crimes, or the sword of the murderer for their estates. (2.) Others of them shall die by famine (<reference osisRef="Job.27.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">His offspring shall not be satisfied with bread.</hi> He thought he had secured to them large estates, but it may happen that they may be reduced to poverty, so as not to have the necessary supports of life, at least not to live comfortably. They shall be so needy that they shall not have a competency of necessary food, and so greedy, or so discontented, that what they have they shall not be satisfied with, because not so much, or not so dainty, as what they have been used to. <hi type="italic">You eat, but you have not enough,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>. (3.) Those that <hi type="italic">remain shall be buried in death,</hi> that is, shall die of the plague, which is called <hi type="italic">death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.8">Rev. vi. 8</reference>), and be buried privately and in haste, as soon as they are dead, without any solemnity, <hi type="italic">buried with the burial of an ass;</hi> and even their <hi type="italic">widows shall not weep;</hi> they shall not have wherewithal to put them in mourning. Or it denotes that these wicked men, as they live undesired, so they die unlamented, and even their widows will think themselves happy that they have got rid of them. <div eID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9907" type="x-p"/> 2. They may prosper in their estates, but ruin attends <hi type="italic">them</hi> too, <reference osisRef="Job.27.16-Job.27.18">v. 16-18</reference>. (1.) We will suppose them to be rich in money and plate, in clothing and furniture. <hi type="italic">They heap up silver</hi> in abundance <hi type="italic">as the dust,</hi> and <hi type="italic">prepare raiment as the clay;</hi> they have heaps of clothes about them, as plentiful as heaps of clay. Or it intimates that they have such abundance of clothes that they are even a burden to them. <hi type="italic">They lade themselves with thick clay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Hab. ii. 6</reference>. See what is the care and business of worldly people—to heap up worldly wealth. Much would have more, until the silver is cankered and the garments are moth-eaten, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.2-Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 2, 3</reference>. But what comes of it? He shall never be the better for it himself; death will strip him, death will rob him, if he be not robbed and stripped sooner, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>. Nay, God will so order it that <hi type="italic">the just shall wear his raiment and the innocent shall divide his silver.</hi> [1.] They shall have it, and divide it among themselves. In some way or other Providence shall so order it that good men shall come honestly by that wealth which the wicked man came dishonestly by. <hi type="italic">The wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Prov. xiii. 22</reference>. God disposes of men's estates as he pleases, and often makes their wills against their wills. The just, whom he hated and persecuted, shall have rule over all his labour, and, in due time, recover with interest what was violently taken from him. The Egyptians' jewels were the Israelites' pay. Solomon observes (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>) that God makes the sinners drudges to the righteous; for the <hi type="italic">sinner he gives travail to gather and heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God.</hi> [2.] They shall do good with it. The innocent shall not hoard the silver, as he did that gathered it, but shall divide it to the poor, shall <hi type="italic">give a portion to seven and also to eight,</hi> which is laying up the best securities. Money is like manure, good for nothing if it be not spread. When God enriches good men they must remember they are but stewards and must give an account. What bad men bring a curse upon their families with the ill-getting of good men bring a blessing upon their families with the well-using of. <hi type="italic">He that by unjust gain increaseth his substance shall gather it for him that will pity the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.8">Prov. xxviii. 8</reference>. (2.) We will suppose them to have built themselves strong and stately houses; but they are like the house which the moth makes for herself in an old garment, out of which she will soon be shaken, <reference osisRef="Job.27.18">v. 18</reference>. He is very secure in it, as a moth, and has no apprehension of danger; but it will prove of as short continuance as <hi type="italic">a booth which the keeper makes,</hi> which will quickly be taken down and gone, and his place shall know him no more. <div eID="gen9907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> 3. Destruction attends their persons, though they lived long in health and at ease (<reference osisRef="Job.27.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The rich man shall lie down</hi> to sleep, to repose himself in the abundance of his wealth (<hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease</hi>), shall lie down in it as his strong city, and seem to others to be very happy and very easy; <hi type="italic">but he shall not be gathered,</hi> that is, he shall not have his mind composed, and settled, and gathered in, to enjoy his wealth. He does not sleep so contentedly as people think he does. He <hi type="italic">lies down,</hi> but <hi type="italic">his abundance will not suffer him to sleep,</hi> at least not so sweetly as the <hi type="italic">labouring man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Eccl. v. 12</reference>. He lies down, but he is full of tossings to and fro till the dawning of the day, and then <hi type="italic">he opens his eyes and he is not;</hi> he sees himself, and all he has, hastening away, as it were, in the twinkling of an eye. His cares increase his fears, and both together make him uneasy, so that, when we attend him to his bed, we do not find him happy there. But, in the close, we are called to attend his exit, and see how miserable he is in death and after death. <div eID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> (1.) He is miserable in death. It is to him the king of terrors, <reference osisRef="Job.27.20-Job.27.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. When some mortal disease seizes him what a fright is he in! <hi type="italic">Terrors take hold of him as waters,</hi> as if he were surrounded by the flowing tides. He trembles to think of leaving this world, and much more of removing to another. This mingles <hi type="italic">sorrow and wrath with his sickness,</hi> as Solomon observes, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Eccl. v. 17</reference>. These terrors put him either [1.] Into a silent and sullen despair; and then the tempest of God's wrath, the tempest of death, may be said <hi type="italic">to steal him away in the night,</hi> when no one is aware or takes any notice of it. Or, [2.] Into an open and clamorous despair; and then he is said <hi type="italic">to be carried away,</hi> and hurled out of his place as with a storm, and with an east wind, violent, and noisy, and very dreadful. Death, to a godly man, is like a fair gale of wind to convey him to the heavenly country, but, to a wicked man, it is like an east wind, a storm, a tempest, that hurries him away in confusion and amazement, to destruction. <div eID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> (2.) He is miserable after death. [1.] His soul falls under the just indignation of God, and it is the terror of that indignation which puts him into such amazement at the approach of death (<reference osisRef="Job.27.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">For God shall cast upon him and not spare.</hi> While he lived he had the benefit of sparing mercy; but now the day of God's patience is over, and he will not spare, but pour out upon him the full vials of his wrath. What God casts down upon a man there is no flying from nor bearing up under. We read of his <hi type="italic">casting down great stones from heaven</hi> upon the Canaanites (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.11">Josh. x. 11</reference>), which made terrible execution among them; but what was that to his casting down his anger in its full weight upon the sinner's conscience, like the <hi type="italic">talent of lead?</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.5.7-Zech.5.8">Zech. v. 7, 8</reference>. The damned sinner, seeing the wrath of God break in upon him, would fain flee out of his hand; but he cannot: the gates of hell are locked and barred, and the great gulf fixed, and it will be in vain to call for the shelter of rocks and mountains. Those who will not be persuaded now to fly to the arms of divine grace, which are stretched out to receive them, will not be able to flee from the arms of divine wrath, which will shortly be stretched out to destroy them. [2.] His memory falls under the just indignation of all mankind (<reference osisRef="Job.27.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Men shall clap their hands at him,</hi> that is, they shall rejoice in the judgments of God, by which he is cut off, and be well pleased in his fall. <hi type="italic">When the wicked perish there is shouting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.10">Prov. xi. 10</reference>. When God buries him men shall hiss him out of his place, and leave on his name perpetual marks of infamy. In the same place where he has been caressed and cried up he shall be laughed at (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>) and his ashes shall be trampled on.  <chapter eID="Job.27"/> <div eID="gen9910" type="x-p"/>

entries.181e07b67c2ea80c13e9ca0b9f885f18ed99aee4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5018"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <div sID="gen7430" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.27.1-Job.27.23">Job 27:1-23</reference>.<div eID="gen7430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7431" type="x-p"/> It was now Zophar's turn to speak. But as he and the other two were silent, virtually admitting defeat, after a pause Job proceeds.<div eID="gen7431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5018"/><hi type="bold">1. parable--</hi>applied in the East to a figurative sententious embodiment of wisdom in poetic form, a gnome (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.4">Psa 49:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continued--</hi>proceeded to put forth; implying elevation of discourse. <div eID="gen7433" type="x-p"/>
entries.39cee733839147b8119f2bf3b6abf77ef2fda22c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5019"/><div sID="gen7434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5019"/>2. (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.3">1Sa 20:3</reference>).<div eID="gen7434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken away ... judgment--</hi>words unconsciously foreshadowing Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Is 53:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.33">Ac 8:33</reference>). God will not give Job his right, by declaring his innocence.<div eID="gen7435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vexed--</hi>Hebrew, "made bitter" (<reference osisRef="Ruth.1.20">Ru 1:20</reference>). <div eID="gen7436" type="x-p"/>
entries.25ee170d7139300463a4d96db2d9acdc426b276b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5020"/><div sID="gen7437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5020"/>3. Implying Job's knowledge of the fact that the living soul was breathed into man by God (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>). "All the while." But Maurer, "As yet all my breath is in me" (notwithstanding my trials): the reason why I can speak so boldly. <div eID="gen7437" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ab33f40f94db5fa2e48f98cf2374190674fb0b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5021"/><div sID="gen7438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5021"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Job.6.28">Job 6:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.30">30</reference>). The "deceit" would be if he were to admit guilt against the witness of his conscience. <div eID="gen7438" type="x-p"/>
entries.5514be828c76a6c25b4e87efc22b7ccb17853eb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5022"/><div sID="gen7439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5022"/><hi type="bold">5. justify you--</hi>approve of your views.<div eID="gen7439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine integrity--</hi>which you deny, on account of my misfortunes. <div eID="gen7440" type="x-p"/>
entries.49c3b6c9fa128d6bbcea932fb0480f18c51fd9b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5023"/><div sID="gen7441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5023"/>6. Rather, my "heart" (conscience) reproaches "not one of my days," that is, I do not repent of any of my days since I came into existence [Maurer]. <div eID="gen7441" type="x-p"/>
entries.124fbee17add65b8d9180216e3cdbc75b3984499: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5024"/><div sID="gen7442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5024"/><hi type="bold">7. Let ... be--</hi>Let mine enemy be accounted as wicked, that is, He who opposes my asseveration of innocence must be regarded as actuated by criminal hostility. Not a curse on his enemies. <div eID="gen7442" type="x-p"/>
entries.020637ed8962b6042ce925ad5c389db2eb65a58a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5025"/><div sID="gen7443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5025"/>8. "What hope hath the hypocrite, notwithstanding all his gains, when?" &c. "Gained" is antithetic to "taketh away." Umbreit's translation is an unmeaning tautology. "When God cuts off, when He taketh away his life."<div eID="gen7443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taketh away--</hi>literally, "draws out" the soul from the body, which is, as it were, its scabbard (<reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">Psa 104:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.15">Da 7:15</reference>). Job says that he admits what Bildad said (<reference osisRef="Job.8.13">Job 8:13</reference>) and Zophar (<reference osisRef="Job.20.5">Job 20:5</reference>). But he says the very fact of his still calling upon God (<reference osisRef="Job.27.10">Job 27:10</reference>) amid all his trials, which a hypocrite would not dare to do, shows he is no "hypocrite." <div eID="gen7444" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bd78203c20536efc7b4d1facafaf91a8043d3ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5026"/><div sID="gen7445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5026"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Psa 66:18</reference>). <div eID="gen7445" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ae6ce7ae6ae94c4bdec5373568d2c838af212c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5027"/><div sID="gen7446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5027"/>10. Alluding to <reference osisRef="Job.22.26">Job 22:26</reference>.<div eID="gen7446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">always call--</hi>He may do so in times of prosperity in order to be thought religious. But he will not, as I do, call on God in calamities verging on death. Therefore I cannot be a "hypocrite" (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.5">20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.8">Psa 62:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7447" type="x-p"/>
entries.6821f313f5f70f4410cf334f4d598a37ad0c1398: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5028"/><div sID="gen7448" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5028"/>11-23. These words are contrary to Job's previous sentiments (see on <reference osisRef="Job.21.22-Job.21.33">Job 21:22-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.22-Job.24.25">Job 24:22-25</reference>). Job 21:22-33; 24:<reference osisRef="Job.33.22-Job.33.25">22-25</reference>). They therefore seem to be Job's statement, not so much of his own sentiments, as of what Zophar would have said had he spoken when his turn came (end of the twenty-sixth chapter). So Job stated the friends' opinion (<reference osisRef="Job.21.17-Job.21.24">Job 21:17-21; 24</reference>:<reference osisRef="Job.21.18-Job.21.21">18-21</reference>). The objection is, why, if so, does not Job answer Zophar's opinion, as stated by himself? The fact is, it is probable that Job tacitly, by giving, in the twenty-eighth chapter, only a general answer, implies, that in spite of the wicked often dying, as he said, in prosperity, he does not mean to deny that the wicked are in the main dealt with according to right, and that God herein vindicates His moral government even here. Job therefore states Zophar's argument more strongly than Zophar would have done. But by comparing <reference osisRef="Job.27.13">Job 27:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference> ("portion," "heritage"), it will be seen, it is Zophar's argument, rather than his own, that Job states. Granting it to be true, implies Job, you ought not to use it as an argument to criminate me. For (<reference osisRef="Job.28.1-Job.28.28">Job 28:1-28</reference>) the ways of divine wisdom in afflicting the godly are inscrutable: all that is sure to man is, the fear of the Lord is wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>).<div eID="gen7448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the hand--</hi>rather, concerning the hand of God, namely, what God does in governing men.<div eID="gen7449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the Almighty--</hi>the counsel or principle which regulates God's dealings. <div eID="gen7450" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a99c14e3b0d288aeb02a7c47ce121d50352bd4d: <div eID="gen17155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17156" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17157" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17157" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17156" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17158" type="x-p"/> Job strongly asserts his innocence; determines to maintain it, and to avoid every evil way, <reference osisRef="Job.27.1-Job.27.7">Job 27:1-7</reference>. Shows his abhorrence of the hypocrite by describing his infamous character, accumulated miseries, and wretched end, vv. 8-23. <div eID="gen17158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17159" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17160" type="x-p"/> Continued his parable - After having delivered the preceding discourse, Job appears to have paused to see if any of his friends chose to make any reply; but finding them all silent, he resumed his discourse, which is here called משלו meshalo, his parable, his authoritative weighty discourse; from משל mashal, to exercise rule, authority, dominion, or power - Parkhurst. And it must be granted that in this speech he assumes great boldness, exhibits his own unsullied character, and treats his friends with little ceremony.
entries.ae01eea763425abe232ba7ac515a7d4935d22296: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17161" type="x-p"/> Who hath taken away my judgment - Who has turned aside my cause, and has not permitted it to come to a hearing, where I might have justice done to me, but has abandoned me to the harsh and uncharitable judgment of my enemies? There appears to be a great want of reverence in these words of Job; he speaks with a degree of irritation, if not bitterness, which cannot be justified. No man should speak thus of his Maker.
entries.e954d143efd4a59b2b7861309f417cbb369a1f55: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17162" type="x-p"/> All the while my breath is in me - As Job appears to allude to the creation of Adam, whom God made out of the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, so that he became a living soul, the whole of Job's assertion may be no more than a periphrasis for As long as I live and have my understanding. Indeed נשמתי nishmathi may be rendered my mind or understanding, and רוח אלוה ruach Eloah, the breath of God, the principle of animal life, the same that he breathed into Adam; for it is there said, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>, He breathed into his nostrils, נשמת חיים nismath chaiyim, the breath of lives, or that principle from which animal and spiritual life proceeds; in consequence of which he became לנפש חיה lenephesh chaiyah, an intelligent or rational animal.
entries.6059f21629a44af278e6739a2bfec8d0be52e821: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17163" type="x-p"/> My lips shall not speak wickedness - As I have hitherto lived in all good conscience before God, as he knoweth, so will I continue to live.
entries.828195eecdc7131148c1d51e9e7acb580f52f035: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17164" type="x-p"/> God forbid - חלילה לי - di chalilah lli, far be it from me, that I should justify you - that I should now, by any kind of acknowledgment of wickedness or hypocrisy justify your harsh judgment. You say that God afflicts me for my crimes; I say, and God knows it is truth, that I have not sinned so as to draw down any such judgment upon me. Your judgment, therefore, is pronounced at your own risk.
entries.2d51f685e41e2405ee2f000b197836a2a9183c5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17165" type="x-p"/> My righteousness I hold fast - I stand firmly on this ground; I have endeavored to live an upright life, and my afflictions are not the consequence of my sins. <div eID="gen17165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17166" type="x-p"/> My heart shall not reproach me - I shall take care so to live that I shall have a conscience void of offense before God and man. "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God;" <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.21">1Jn 3:21</reference>. This seems to be Job's meaning.
entries.8ff622d886676d06525e7dcc3c3cf2448dbdda12: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17167" type="x-p"/> Let mine enemy be as the wicked - Let my accuser be proved a lying and perjured man, because he has laid to my charge things which he cannot prove, and which are utterly false.
entries.b3e5460fc08ccccd4777b57b384873dea08366ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17168" type="x-p"/> What is the hope of the hypocrite - The word חנף chaneph, which we translate, most improperly, hypocrite, means a wicked fellow, a defiled, polluted wretch, a rascal, a knave, a man who sticks at nothing in order to gain his ends. In this verse it means a dishonest man, a rogue, who by overreaching, cheating, etc., has amassed a fortune. <div eID="gen17168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17169" type="x-p"/> When God taketh away his soul? - Could he have had any well grounded hope of eternal blessedness when he was acquiring earthly property by guilt and deceit? And of what avail will this property be when his soul is summoned before the judgment-seat? A righteous man yields up his soul to God; the wicked does not, because he is afraid of God, of death, and of eternity. God therefore takes the soul away - forces it out of the body. Mr. Blair gives us an affecting picture of the death of a wicked man. Though well known, I shall insert it as a striking comment on this passage: - "How shocking must thy summons be, O death! <div eID="gen17169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17170" type="x-p"/> To him that is at ease in his possessions; <div eID="gen17170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17171" type="x-p"/> Who, counting on long years of pleasures here; <div eID="gen17171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17172" type="x-p"/> Is quite unfurnished for that world to come! <div eID="gen17172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17173" type="x-p"/> In that dread moment how the frantic soul <div eID="gen17173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17174" type="x-p"/> Raves round the walls of her clay tenement; <div eID="gen17174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17175" type="x-p"/> Runs to each avenue, and shrieks for help, <div eID="gen17175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17176" type="x-p"/> But shrieks in vain! How wishfully she looks <div eID="gen17176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17177" type="x-p"/> On all she's leaving, now no longer hers! <div eID="gen17177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17178" type="x-p"/> A little longer, yet a little longer, <div eID="gen17178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17179" type="x-p"/> O, might she stay, to wash away her stains, <div eID="gen17179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17180" type="x-p"/> And fit her for her passage! Mournful sight! <div eID="gen17180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17181" type="x-p"/> Her very eyes weep blood; and every groan <div eID="gen17181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17182" type="x-p"/> She heaves is big with horror. But the foe, <div eID="gen17182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17183" type="x-p"/> Like a stanch murderer, steady to his purpose, <div eID="gen17183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17184" type="x-p"/> Pursues her close, through every lane of life, <div eID="gen17184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17185" type="x-p"/> Nor misses once the track, but presses on; <div eID="gen17185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17186" type="x-p"/> Till, forced at last to the tremendous verge, <div eID="gen17186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17187" type="x-p"/> At once she sinks to everlasting ruin." <div eID="gen17187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17188" type="x-p"/> The Grave. <div eID="gen17188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17189" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee has, What can the detractor expect who has gathered together (ממון דשקר mamon dishkar, the mammon of unrighteousness) when God plucks out his soul? The Septuagint: Τις γαρ εστιν ετι ελπις ασεβει, ὁτι επεχει; Μη πεποιθως επι Κυριον ει αρα σωθησεται; "For what is the hope of the ungodly that he should wait for? shall he, by hoping in the Lord, be therefore saved?" Mr. Good translates differently from all the versions: - "Yet what is the hope of the wicked that he should prosper, <div eID="gen17189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17190" type="x-p"/> That God should keep his soul in quiet?" <div eID="gen17190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17191" type="x-p"/> I believe our version gives as true a sense as any; and the words appear to have been in the eye of our Lord, when he said, "For what is a man profited if he shall gain the whole world and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?" <reference osisRef="Mat.16.26">Mat 16:26</reference>.
entries.f31eb9a7fbdfe78091615cdd3c7b07dc36635184: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17192" type="x-p"/> I will teach you by the hand of God - Relying on Divine assistance, and not speaking out of my own head, or quoting what others have said I will teach you what the mind of the Almighty is, and I will conceal nothing. Job felt that the good hand of his God was upon him, and that therefore he should make no mistake in his doctrines. In this way the Chaldee understood the words, ביד אל beyad El, by the hand of God, which it translates בנבואת אלהא binbuath Elaha, by the prophecy of God. Those who reject the literal meaning, which conveys a very good sense, may adopt the translation of Mr. Good, which has much to recommend it: "I will teach you concerning the dealings of God."
entries.321090f3040685d319271503d38324fc9c8ec9d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17193" type="x-p"/> Ye yourselves have seen it - Your own experience and observation have shown you that the righteous are frequently in affliction, and the wicked in affluence. <div eID="gen17193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17194" type="x-p"/> Why then are ye thus altogether vain? - The original is very emphatical: הבל תהבלו hebel tehbalu, and well expressed by Mr. Good: "Why then should ye thus babble babblings!" It our language would allow it, we might say vanitize vanity.
entries.7aefadfb00289a411ce74b0a369a6f7dd57876b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17195" type="x-p"/> This is the portion of a wicked man - Job now commences his promised teaching; and what follows is a description of the lot or portion of the wicked man and of tyrants. And this remuneration shall they have with God in general, though the hand of man be not laid upon them. Though he does not at all times show his displeasure against the wicked, by reducing them to a state of poverty and affliction, yet he often does it so that men may see it; and at other times he seems to pass them by, reserving their judgment for another world, that men may not forget that there is a day of judgment and perdition for ungodly men, and a future recompense for the righteous.
entries.58965d0a54bb7d115ab364b91b39a09a3c41122c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17196" type="x-p"/> If his children be multiplied - As numerous families were supposed to be a proof of the benediction of the Almighty, Job shows that this is not always the case; for the offspring of the wicked shall be partly cut off by violent deaths, and partly reduced to great poverty.
entries.add5d30f67f1f06c9636a80c43a5544c92b19883: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17197" type="x-p"/> Those that remain of him - שרידיו seridaiv, his remains, whether meaning himself personally, or his family. <div eID="gen17197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17198" type="x-p"/> Shall be buried in death - Shall come to utter and remediless destruction. Death shall have his full conquest over them, and the grave its complete victory. These are no common dead. All the sting, all the wound, and all the poison of sin, remains: and so evident are God's judgments in his and their removal, that even widows shall not weep for them; the public shall not bewail them; for when the wicked perish there is shouting. Mr. Good, following the Chaldee, translates: Entombed in corruption, or in the pestilence. But I see no reason why we should desert the literal reading. Entombed in corruption gives no nervous sense in my judgment; for in corruption are the high and the low, the wicked and the good, entombed: but buried in death is at once nervous and expressive. Death itself is the place where he shall lie; he shall have no redemption, no resurrection to life; death shall ever have dominion over him. The expression is very similar to that in <reference osisRef="Luk.16.22">Luk 16:22</reference> (note), as found in several versions and MSS.: The rich man died, and was buried in hell; and, lifting up his eyes, being in torment, he saw, etc. See my note there.
entries.2b9cd81eebaed8a766cd80d1b8876d7319e6e7b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17199" type="x-p"/> Though he heap up silver - Though he amass riches in the greatest abundance, he shall not enjoy them. Unsanctified wealth is a curse to its possessor. Money, of all earthly possessions, is the most dangerous, as it is the readiest agent to do good or evil. He that perverts it is doubly cursed, because it affords him the most immediate means of sinful gratification; and he can sin more in an hour through this, than he can in a day or week by any other kind of property. On the other hand, they who use it aright have it in their power to do the most prompt and immediate good. Almost every kind of want may be speedily relieved by it. Hence, he who uses it as he ought is doubly blessed; while he who abuses it is doubly cursed.
entries.711a934775d0525a380ed6acab72e2f6321ac687: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17200" type="x-p"/> The just shall put it on - Money is God's property. "The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the Lord;" and though it may be abused for a time by unrighteous hands, God, in the course of his providence, brings it back to its proper use; and often the righteous possess the inheritance of the wicked.
entries.fde2b4fbd9867f69374052e414ec3680e65226fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17201" type="x-p"/> He buildeth his house as a moth - With great skill, great pains, and great industry; but the structure, however skillful, shall be dissolved; and the materials, however costly, shall be brought to corruption. To its owner it shall be only a temporary habitation, like that which the moth makes in its larve or caterpillar state, during its change from a chrysalis to a winged insect. <div eID="gen17201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17202" type="x-p"/> As a booth that the keeper maketh - A shed which the watchman or keeper of a vineyard erects to cover him from the scorching sun, while watching the ripening grapes, that they may be preserved from depredation. Travellers in the East have observed that such booths or sheds are made of the lightest and most worthless materials; and after the harvest or vintage is in, they are quite neglected, and by the winter rains, etc., are soon dissolved and destroyed.
entries.ddcb10130fb9bf56ba2e4f1efe454af3b7877aa9: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen17202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17203" type="x-p"/> The rich man shall lie down - In the grave. But he shall not be gathered - Neither have a respectable burial among men, nor be gathered with the righteous in the kingdom of God. It may be that Job alludes here to an opinion relative to the state of certain persons after death, prevalent in all nations in ancient times, viz., that those whose funeral rites had not been duly performed, wander about as ghosts, and find no rest. <div eID="gen17203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17204" type="x-p"/> He openeth his eyes - In the morning of the resurrection. <div eID="gen17204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17205" type="x-p"/> And he is not - He is utterly lost and undone for ever. This seems to be the plain sense of the passage; and so all the versions appear to have understood it; but Reiske and some others, by making יאסף yeaseph an Arabic word, signifying, not the idea of gathering, but care, anxiety, etc., have quite altered this sense of the passage; and Mr. Good, who copies them, translates thus: Let the rich man lie down, and care not. I see no manner of occasion to resort to this interpretation, which, in my judgment, gives a sense inferior to that given above, or to the following: The rich man shall lie down - go to his rest, fully persuaded that his property is in perfect safety; but he shall not be gathered, or he shall not gather - make any farther addition to his stores: he openeth his eyes in the morning, when he is not - marauders in the night have stripped him of all his property, as in the case of Job himself; a case quite probable, and not unfrequent in Arabia, when a hostile tribe makes a sudden incursion, and carries off an immense booty. But I prefer the first meaning, as it is obtained without crucifying the text. Coverdale translates: When the rich man dyeth, he carieth nothinge with him: he is gone in the twincklinge of an eye.
entries.f9bee9ee8da4fe537910acfe7e5cc0452c1e7075: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17206" type="x-p"/> Terrors take hold on him as waters - They come upon him as an irresistible flood; and he is overwhelmed as by a tempest in the night, when darkness partly hides his danger, and deprives him of discerning the way to escape.
entries.abdb237338b79f2d82511ec9b77326e518b83c72: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17207" type="x-p"/> The east wind carrieth him away - Such as is called by Mr. Good, a levanter, the euroclydon, the eastern storm of <reference osisRef="Act.27.14">Act 27:14</reference>.
entries.f4f7c35d0ece0834609a0098b7a17241285d9ae7: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17208" type="x-p"/> God shall cast upon him - Or, rather, the storm mentioned above shall incessantly pelt him, and give him no respite; nor can he by any means escape from its fury.
entries.5f5d4d4032cd97e6e8f58a0931b19905bb9cf584: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17209" type="x-p"/> Men shall clap their hands at him - These two verses refer to the storm, which is to sweep away the ungodly; therefore the word God, in <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">Job 27:22</reference>, and men in this verse, should be omitted. <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">Job 27:22</reference> : "For it shall fall upon him, and not spare: flying from its power he shall continue to fly. <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>. It shall clap its hands against him, and hiss, וישרק veyishrok, shriek, him out of his place." <div eID="gen17209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17210" type="x-p"/> Here the storm is personified and the wicked actor is hissed and driven by it from off the stage. It seems it was an ancient method to clap the hands against and hiss a man from any public office, who had acted improperly in it. The populace, in European countries, express their disapprobation of public characters who have not pleased them in the same manner to the present day, by hisses, groans, and the like.  <chapter eID="Job.27"/> <div eID="gen17210" type="x-p"/>

entries.91cd43a8310b34ba2fc2157b797e219250fd4bd0: <reference osisRef="Job.27.1-Job.7.1">Job 27:1-7   1</reference>  Then Job continued to take up his proverb, and said:   2  As God liveth, who hath deprived me of my right, <div eID="gen8006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8007" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty, who hath sorely saddened my soul -   3  For still all my breath is in me, <div eID="gen8007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8008" type="x-p"/> And the breath of Eloah in my nostrils -   4  My lips do not speak what is false, <div eID="gen8008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8009" type="x-p"/> And my tongue uttereth not deceit!   5  Far be it from me, to grant that you are in the right: <div eID="gen8009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8010" type="x-p"/> Till I die I will not remove my innocence from me.   6  My righteousness I hold fast, and let it not go: <div eID="gen8010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8011" type="x-p"/> My heart reproacheth not any of my days.   7  Mine enemy must appear as an evil-doer, <div eID="gen8011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8012" type="x-p"/> And he who riseth up against me as unrighteous. <div eID="gen8012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8013" type="x-p"/> The friends are silent, Job remains master of the discourse, and his continued speech is introduced as a continued שׂאת משׁלו (after the analogy of the phrase נשׂא קול), as in Num 23:7 and further on, the oracles of Balaam. משׁל is speech of a more elevated tone and more figurative character; here, as frequently, the unaffected outgrowth of an elevated solemn mood. The introduction of the ultimatum, as משׁל, reminds one of “the proverb (<hi type="italic">el - methel</hi>) seals it” in the mouth of the Arab, since in common life it is customary to use a pithy saying as the final proof at the conclusion of a speech. <div eID="gen8013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8014" type="x-p"/> Job begins with an asseveration of his truthfulness (i.e., the agreement of his confession with his consciousness) by the life of God. From this oath, which in the form <hi type="italic">bi - hajât allâh</hi> has become later on a common formula of assurance, R. Joshua, in his tractate <hi type="italic">Sota</hi>, infers that Job served God from love to Him, for we only swear by the life of that which we honour and love; it is more natural to conclude that the God by whom on the one hand, he believes himself to be so unjustly treated, still appears to him, on the other hand, to be the highest manifestation of truth. The interjectional clause: living is God! is equivalent to, as true as God liveth. That which is affirmed is not what immediately follows: He has set aside my right, and the Almighty has sorely grieved my soul (Raschi); but הסיר משׁפטי and המר נפשׁי are attributive clauses, by which what is denied in the form of an oath introduced by אם (as <reference osisRef="Gen.42.15">Gen 42:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.45">1Sa 14:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.11">2Sa 11:11</reference>, Ges. §155, 2, <hi type="italic">f</hi>) is contained in <reference osisRef="Job.27.4">Job 27:4</reference>; his special reference to the false semblance of an evil-doer shows that semblance which suffering casts upon him, but which he constantly repudiates as surely not lying, as that God liveth. Among moderns, Schlottm. (comp. Ges. §150, 3), like most of the old expositors, translates: so long as my breath is in me,...my lips shall speak no wrong, so that <reference osisRef="Job.27.3">Job 27:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.27.4">Job 27:4</reference> together contain what is affirmed. By (1) כּי indeed sometimes introduces that which shall happen as affirmed by oath, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.5">Jer 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">Jer 49:13</reference>; but here that which shall not take place is affirmed, which would be introduced first in a general form by כּי <hi type="italic">explic. s. recitativum, </hi>then according to its special negative contents by אם, - a construction which is perhaps possible according to syntax, but it is nevertheless perplexing; (2) it may perhaps be thought that “the whole continuance of my breath in me” is conceived as accusative and adverbial, and is equivalent to, so long as my breath may remain in me (כל עוד, as long as ever, like the Arab. <hi type="italic">cullama</hi>, as often as ever); but the usage of the language does not favour this explanation, for <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.9">2Sa 1:9</reference>, נפשׁי בי כל־עוד, signifies my whole soul (my full life) is still in me; and we have a third instance of this prominently placed כל <hi type="italic">per hypallagen</hi> in Hos 14:3, עון כל־תשׂא, <hi type="italic">omnem auferas iniquitatem,</hi> Ew. §289, <hi type="italic">a</hi> (comp. Ges. §114, rem. 1). Accordingly, with Ew., Hirz., Hahn, and most modern expositors, we take <reference osisRef="Job.27.3">Job 27:3</reference> as a parenthetical confirmatory clause, by which Job gives the ground of his solemn affirmation that he is still in possession of his full consciousness, and cannot help feeling and expressing the contradiction between his lot of suffering, which brand shim as an evil-doer, and his moral integrity. The נשׁמתי which precedes the רוח signifies, according to the prevailing usage of the language, the intellectual, and therefore self-conscious, soul of man (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 76f.). This is in man and in his nostrils, inasmuch as the breath which passes in and out by these is the outward and visible form of its being, which is in every respect the condition of life (<hi type="italic">ib.</hi> S. 82f.). The suff. of נשׁמתי is unaccented; on account of the word which follows being a monosyllable, the tone has retreated (נסוג אחור, to use a technical grammatical expression), as e.g., also in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.2">Job 20:2</reference>; Psa 22:20. Because he lives, and, living, cannot deny his own existence, he swears that his own testimony, which is suspected by the friends, and on account of which they charge him with falsehood, is perfect truth. <div eID="gen8014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8015" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.27.4">Job 27:4</reference> is not to be translated: “my lips shall never speak what is false;” for it is not a resolve which Job thus strongly makes, after the manner of a vow, but the agreement of his confession, which he has now so frequently made, and which remains unalterable, with the abiding fact. Far be from me - he continues in <reference osisRef="Job.27.5">Job 27:5</reference> - to admit that you are right (חלילה לּי with unaccented <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, not of the <hi type="italic">fem.,</hi> comp. <reference osisRef="Job.34.10">Job 34:10</reference>, but of direction: for a profanation to me, i.e., let it be profane to me, Ew. §329, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">hâshâ li ,</hi> in the like sense); until I expire (prop.: sink together), I will not put my innocence (תּמּה, perfection, in the sense of purity of character) away from me, i.e., I will not cease from asserting it. I will hold fast (as ever) my righteousness, and leave it not, i.e., let it not go or fall away; my heart does not reproach even one of my days. מיּמי is virtually an obj. in a partitive sense: <hi type="italic">mon coeur ne me reproche pas un seul de mes jours</hi> (Renan). The heart is used here as the seat of the conscience, which is the knowledge possessed by the heart, by which it excuses or accuses a man (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 134); חרף (whence חרף, the season in which the fruits are gathered) signifies <hi type="italic">carpere</hi>, to pluck = to pinch, lash, inveigh against. Jos. Kimchi and Ralbag explain: my heart draws not back) from the confession of my innocence) my whole life long (as Maimonides explains נחרפת, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.20">Lev 19:20</reference>, of the female slave who is inclined to, i.e., stands near to, the position of a free woman), by comparison with the Arabic <hi type="italic">inḥarafa , deflectere;</hi> it is not, however, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥrf ,</hi> but <hi type="italic">chrf , decerpere,</hi> that is to be compared in the tropical sense of the prevailing usage of the Hebrew specified. The old expositors were all misled by the misunderstood partitive מימי, which they translated <hi type="italic">ex</hi> (= <hi type="italic">inde a</hi>) <hi type="italic">diebus meis</hi>. There is in <reference osisRef="Job.27.7">Job 27:7</reference> no ground for taking יהי, with Hahn, as a strong affirmative, as supposed in <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>, and not as expressive of desire; but the meaning is not: let my opponents be evil-doers, I at least am not one (Hirz.). The voluntative expresses far more emotion: the relation must be reversed; he who will brand me as an evil-doer, must by that very act brand himself as such, inasmuch as the מרשׁיע of a צדיק really shows himself to be a רשׁע, and by recklessly judging the righteous, is bringing down upon himself a like well-merited judgment. The כּ is the so-called <hi type="italic">Caph veritatis, </hi>since כּ, <hi type="italic">instar,</hi> signifies not only similarity, but also quality. Instead of קימי, the less manageable, primitive form, which the poet used in <reference osisRef="Job.22.20">Job 22:20</reference> (comp. p. 483), and beside which קם (קום,   2Ki 16:7) does not occur in the book, we here find the more usual form מתקוממי (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.20.27">Job 20:27</reference>).<note placement="foot">In Beduin the enemy is called <hi type="italic">qômâni</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, on <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference>, p. 505), a denominative from <hi type="italic">qôm</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">qawm ,</hi> war, feud; but qôm has also the signification of a collective of <hi type="italic">qômâni</hi>, and one can also say: <hi type="italic">entum wa - ijânâ qôm ,</hi> you and we are enemies, and <hi type="italic">bênâtna qôm ,</hi> there is war between us. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8016" type="x-p"/> The description of the misfortune of the ungodly which now follows, beginning with כי, requires no connecting thought, as for instance: My enemy must be accounted as ungodly, on account of his hostility; I abhor ungodliness, for, etc.; but that he who regards him as a רשׁע is himself a רשׁע, Job shows from the fact of the רשׁע having no hope in death, whilst, when dying, he can give no confident hope of a divine vindication of his innocence.
entries.86c72b4c34fb9837639babd85338d05f06347193: <reference osisRef="Job.27.8-Job.12.8">Job 27:8-12   8</reference>  For what is the hope of the godless, when He cutteth off, <div eID="gen8016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8017" type="x-p"/> When Eloah taketh away his soul?   9  Will God hear his cry <div eID="gen8017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8018" type="x-p"/> When distress cometh upon him? 10  Or can he delight himself in the Almighty, <div eID="gen8018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8019" type="x-p"/> Can he call upon Eloah at all times? 11  I will teach you concerning the hand of God, <div eID="gen8019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8020" type="x-p"/> I will not conceal the dealings of the Almighty. 12  Behold, ye have all seen it, <div eID="gen8020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8021" type="x-p"/> Why then do ye cherish foolish notions? <div eID="gen8021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8022" type="x-p"/> In comparing himself with the רשׁע, Job is conscious that he has a God who does not leave him unheard, in whom he delights himself, and to whom he can at all times draw near; as, in fact, Job’s fellowship with God rests upon the freedom of the most intimate confidence. He is not one of the godless; for what is the hope of one who is estranged from God, when he comes to die? He has no God on whom his hope might establish itself, to whom it could cling. The old expositors err in many ways respecting <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job 27:8</reference>, by taking בצע, <hi type="italic">abscindere</hi> (root בץ), in the sense of (<hi type="italic">opes</hi>) <hi type="italic">corradere</hi> (thus also more recently Rosenm. after the Targ., Syr., and Jer.), and referring ישׁל to שׁלה in the signification <hi type="italic">tranquillum esse</hi> (thus even Blumenfeld after Ralbag and others). נפשׁו is the object to both verbs, and בצע נפשׁ, <hi type="italic">abscindere animam,</hi> to cut off the thread of life, is to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Job.6.9">Job 6:9</reference>; Isa 38:12. שׁלח נפשׁ, <hi type="italic">extrahere animam</hi> (from שׁלה, whence שׁליח Arab. <hi type="italic">salan</hi>, the after-birth, cogn. שׁלל . Arab. <hi type="italic">sll ,</hi> נשׁל Arab. <hi type="italic">nsl , nṯl , nšl</hi>), is of similar signification, according to another figure, wince the body is conceived of as the sheath (נדנה, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.15">Dan 7:15</reference>) of the soul<note placement="foot">On the similar idea of the body, as the <hi type="italic">kosha</hi> (sheath) of the soul, among the Hindus, vid., Psychol. S. 227.</note> (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">sll</hi> in the universal signification <hi type="italic">evaginare ensem</hi>). The <hi type="italic">fut. apoc. Kal</hi> ישׁל (= ישׁל) is therefore in meaning equivalent to the intrans. ישּׁל, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.40">Deu 28:40</reference> (according to Ew. §235, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, obtained from this by change of vowel), <hi type="italic">decidere;</hi> and Schnurrer’s supposition that ישׁל, like the Arab. <hi type="italic">ysl</hi>, is equivalent to ישׁאל (when God demands it), or such a violent correction as De Lagarde's<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Anm. zur griech. Uebers. der Proverbien</hi> (1863), S.
